claim: CCK-expressing cells comprise approximately 5% of l/vlPAG neurons.
source: Quantification showed that CCK-GFP cells comprise approximately 5% of l/vlPAG neurons and are more prevalent in the l/vlPAG than dlPAG (Figure 1C; n = 4, t (3) = 8.743, p=0.0032).
evidence: Supported by quantification data from immunostaining experiments showing CCK-GFP+ and NeuN+ cell counts.

claim: CCK-expressing cells are more prevalent in the l/vlPAG than dlPAG.
source: Quantification showed that CCK-GFP cells comprise approximately 5% of l/vlPAG neurons and are more prevalent in the l/vlPAG than dlPAG (Figure 1C; n = 4, t (3) = 8.743, p=0.0032).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of CCK-GFP cell counts between dlPAG and l/vlPAG regions.

claim: A majority (94.8%) of GFP-labeled CCK cells in the l/vlPAG are also vGlut2-labeled.
source: Notably, we found that a majority of GFP-labeled cells (94.8%) were also vGlut2-labeled (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification showing overlap between GFP and vGlut2 markers.

claim: 9.6% of vGlut2-labeled cells in the l/vlPAG are also GFP-labeled CCK cells.
source: We found that a small fraction (9.6%) of vGlut2-labeled cells were also GFP-labeled (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining quantification data.

claim: 8.58% of vGlut2-expressing cells co-express CCK based on in situ hybridization.
source: Similarly, in situ hybridizations revealed that 8.58% of vGlut2-expressing cells co-express CCK (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data showing mRNA co-expression.

claim: CCK+ cells in the l/vlPAG are primarily glutamatergic.
source: Our characterization shows that CCK+ cells comprise a small, sparse subset of PAG neurons that span the lateral and ventrolateral columns and are primarily glutamatergic.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and in situ hybridization data showing high overlap between CCK and vGlut2 markers.

claim: Activation of dlPAG-syn cells increased speed compared to control mice.
source: Activation of dlPAG-syn cells increased speed and open-field corner entries compared to control mice (Figure 2H and L; dlPAG-eYFP, n = 5; dlPAG-ChR2, n = 4; speed: t(7) = 2.495, p=0.0413; corner entries: t(7) = 2.451, p=0.044).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments with statistical comparison between ChR2 and control groups.

claim: Activation of dlPAG-syn cells increased open-field corner entries compared to control mice.
source: Activation of dlPAG-syn cells increased speed and open-field corner entries compared to control mice (Figure 2H and L; dlPAG-eYFP, n = 5; dlPAG-ChR2, n = 4; speed: t(7) = 2.495, p=0.0413; corner entries: t(7) = 2.451, p=0.044).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments with statistical comparison.

claim: Activation of dlPAG-syn cells induced escape jumping.
source: Notably, activation of only this, but not other PAG populations, induced escape jumping (Figure 2I; dlPAG-YFP, n = 5; dlPAG-ChR2, n = 4; t(7) = 6.111, p=0.0005).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing jumping behavior specific to dlPAG-syn activation.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells strongly promoted freezing.
source: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells strongly promoted freezing, and consequently reduced speed and corner entries (Figure 2H, J and L); (l/vlPAG-syn-eYFP, n = 5; l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2, n = 5; freezing: t(8) = 9.176, p<0.0001; speed: t(8) = 7.741, p < 0.0001; corner entries: t(8) = 4.548, p=0.0019).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments with statistical comparison.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells reduced speed.
source: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells strongly promoted freezing, and consequently reduced speed and corner entries (Figure 2H, J and L); (l/vlPAG-syn-eYFP, n = 5; l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2, n = 5; freezing: t(8) = 9.176, p<0.0001; speed: t(8) = 7.741, p < 0.0001; corner entries: t(8) = 4.548, p=0.0019).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells reduced corner entries.
source: Light activation of l/vlPAG-syn cells strongly promoted freezing, and consequently reduced speed and corner entries (Figure 2H, J and L); (l/vlPAG-syn-eYFP, n = 5; l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2, n = 5; freezing: t(8) = 9.176, p<0.0001; speed: t(8) = 7.741, p < 0.0001; corner entries: t(8) = 4.548, p=0.0019).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased speed.
source: We observed that activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased speed, reduced time spent in the open-field center, and increased corner entries (Figure 2H, K, and L; l/vlPAG-CCK-eYFP, n = 17; l/vlPAG-CCK-ChR2, n = 14; speed: t(29) = 3.667, p=0.001; center time: t(29) = 3.334, p=0.0023; corner entries: t(29) = 5.253, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments with statistical comparison.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells reduced time spent in the open-field center.
source: We observed that activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased speed, reduced time spent in the open-field center, and increased corner entries (Figure 2H, K, and L; l/vlPAG-CCK-eYFP, n = 17; l/vlPAG-CCK-ChR2, n = 14; speed: t(29) = 3.667, p=0.001; center time: t(29) = 3.334, p=0.0023; corner entries: t(29) = 5.253, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased corner entries.
source: We observed that activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased speed, reduced time spent in the open-field center, and increased corner entries (Figure 2H, K, and L; l/vlPAG-CCK-eYFP, n = 17; l/vlPAG-CCK-ChR2, n = 14; speed: t(29) = 3.667, p=0.001; center time: t(29) = 3.334, p=0.0023; corner entries: t(29) = 5.253, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased time spent in the corners of the open field.
source: Interestingly, activation of only this population increased time spent in the corners of the open field (Figure 2M; l/vlPAG-CCK-eYFP, n = 17; l/vlPAG-CCK-ChR2, n = 14; t(29) = 2.967, p=0.006).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing specific corner preference.

claim: Optogenetic activation of l/vlPAG-CCK neurons reduced latency to enter the burrow relative to YFP control mice.
source: Despite similar levels of preference for the burrow during habituation, only optogenetic activation of l/vlPAG-CCK neurons reduced LTE the burrow relative to YFP control mice (Figure 3C–F; l/vlPAG-CCK-eYFP, n = 17; l/vlPAG-CCK-ChR2, n = 14; t(29) = 4.108, p=0.0003).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments in the latency to enter assay.

claim: Activation of syn-expressing l/vlPAG neurons robustly increased latency to enter the burrow as l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2 mice displayed substantial freezing with light-delivery compared to YFP mice.
source: Notably, activation of syn-expressing l/vlPAG neurons robustly increased latency as l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2 mice displayed substantial freezing with light-delivery compared to YFP mice (Figure 3F; l/vlPAG-syn-eYFP, n = 5; l/vlPAG-syn-ChR2, n = 5; t(8) = 3.777, p=0.0054).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing increased latency due to freezing behavior.

claim: Pairing light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells with one of two chambers in the real-time place test assay resulted in avoidance of the stimulated chamber.
source: Pairing light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells with one of two chambers in the real-time place test assay resulted in avoidance of the stimulated chamber, suggesting increased l/vlPAG-CCK activity is aversive (Figure 4A–C; eYFP, n = 14; ChR2, n = 8; t(20) = 4.938, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by real-time place preference test data showing chamber avoidance.

claim: Increased l/vlPAG-CCK activity is aversive.
source: Pairing light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells with one of two chambers in the real-time place test assay resulted in avoidance of the stimulated chamber, suggesting increased l/vlPAG-CCK activity is aversive (Figure 4A–C; eYFP, n = 14; ChR2, n = 8; t(20) = 4.938, p<0.0001).
evidence: Inferred from avoidance behavior in real-time place preference test.

claim: Stimulation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells in the elevated plus maze reduced time spent in the open arms of the maze.
source: Furthermore, stimulation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells in the elevated plus maze (EPM) reduced time spent in the open arms of the maze (Figure 4D–F; eYFP, n = 16; ChR2, n = 10; t(24) = 3.391, p=0.0024).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments in the elevated plus maze.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells markedly increased pupil size.
source: Light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells also markedly increased pupil size, a hallmark sympathetic response (Figure 4G and H; eYFP, n = 4; ChR2, n = 7; t(9) = 2.908, p=0.0174).
evidence: Supported by pupil size measurements during optogenetic activation.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK cell activation is aversive, anxiogenic, and may elicit sympathetic activation.
source: Together, these results suggest that l/vlPAG-CCK cell activation is aversive, anxiogenic, and may elicit sympathetic activation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple behavioral and physiological measures including place avoidance, reduced open arm time, and increased pupil size.

claim: Light inhibition of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased latency to enter the burrow in Arch mice compared to eGFP control mice.
source: Though burrow preference was similar across both groups during habituation, light inhibition of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased LTE the burrow in Arch mice compared to eGFP control mice (Figure 5C–F; GFP, n = 6; Arch, n = 7; t(11) = 2.447, p=0.0324).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments in the latency to enter assay.

claim: Activity in l/vlPAG-CCK cells can bidirectionally control flight to a dark burrow under low-threat conditions.
source: Thus, in addition to our activation studies, we show activity in l/vlPAG-CCK cells can bidirectionally control flight to a dark burrow under low-threat conditions.
evidence: Supported by both activation and inhibition experiments showing opposite effects on burrow entry latency.

claim: Mice exhibit robust defensive reactions during exposure to a live rat but not a similarly shaped toy rat such as increased freezing, increased distance from the live rat, and reduced time in the zone containing the live rat.
source: Rats are natural predators of mice, and mice exhibit robust defensive reactions during exposure to a live rat but not a similarly shaped toy rat such as increased freezing, increased distance from the live rat, and reduced time in the zone containing the live rat (Figure 6B; n = 10; freezing: t(9) = 3.519, p=0.0065; threat distance: t(9) = 13.09, p<0.0001; threat zone: t(9) = 7.604, p<0.0001; Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by behavioral measurements comparing live rat versus toy rat exposure.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells reduced time spent in the threat zone during live rat exposure.
source: Light activation of CCK+ cells reduced time spent in the threat zone and increased distance from the live rat (Figure 6F and G; eYFP, n = 10; ChR2, n = 9; time in threat zone: t(17) = 3.808, p=0.0014; distance: t(17) = 3.24, p=0.0048).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments during live predator exposure.

claim: Light activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells increased distance from the live rat.
source: Light activation of CCK+ cells reduced time spent in the threat zone and increased distance from the live rat (Figure 6F and G; eYFP, n = 10; ChR2, n = 9; time in threat zone: t(17) = 3.808, p=0.0014; distance: t(17) = 3.24, p=0.0048).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments during live predator exposure.

claim: Optogenetic activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells reduced stretch-attend postures during live rat exposure.
source: This measure was reduced as a result of optogenetic activation, demonstrating that not all defensive behaviors are promoted by CCK+ cell activation (Figure 6I; eYFP, n = 10; ChR2, n = 9; t(17) = 2.441, p=0.0259).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments measuring stretch-attend behavior.

claim: Optogenetic activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells did not alter freezing during live rat exposure.
source: Optogenetic activation of CCK+ cells also induced a trend toward reduced number of approaches toward the rat and did not alter freezing or locomotion (Figure 6H, J, and K; eYFP, n = 10; ChR2, n = 9; approaches: t(17) = 1.965, p=0.066; freezing: t(17) = 0.4696, p=0.6446; locomotion: t(17) = 1.682, p=0.1109).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing no significant change in freezing.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells selectively enhanced avoidance of a live predator without altering freezing.
source: These results demonstrate that activation of l/vlPAG-CCK cells selectively enhanced avoidance of a live predator without altering freezing.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments showing increased avoidance measures but no change in freezing.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition significantly increased time spent in the threat zone during live rat exposure.
source: We found that l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition significantly increased time spent in the threat zone, increased the number of approaches toward the rat, and reduced escape velocity from the rat (Figure 7D, F and H; threat zone: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.554, p=0.0199; approaches: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.194, p=0.0496; escape velocity: mCherry, n = 7; hM4Di, n = 11; t(16) = 2.197, p=0.0431).
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments during live predator exposure.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition increased the number of approaches toward the rat.
source: We found that l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition significantly increased time spent in the threat zone, increased the number of approaches toward the rat, and reduced escape velocity from the rat (Figure 7D, F and H; threat zone: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.554, p=0.0199; approaches: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.194, p=0.0496; escape velocity: mCherry, n = 7; hM4Di, n = 11; t(16) = 2.197, p=0.0431).
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition reduced escape velocity from the rat.
source: We found that l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition significantly increased time spent in the threat zone, increased the number of approaches toward the rat, and reduced escape velocity from the rat (Figure 7D, F and H; threat zone: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.554, p=0.0199; approaches: mCherry, n = 8; hM4Di, n = 12; t(18) = 2.194, p=0.0496; escape velocity: mCherry, n = 7; hM4Di, n = 11; t(16) = 2.197, p=0.0431).
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition did not affect avoidance from a toy rat.
source: Importantly, l/vlPAG-CCK inhibition did not affect avoidance from a toy rat (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–I), indicating that the effects of inhibition are specific to a live predator.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments during toy rat exposure showing no significant effects.

claim: Inhibition of l/vlPAG-CCK cells did not affect pain response latency during exposure to a heated plate assay.
source: Inhibition of CCK cells also did not affect pain response latency during exposure to a heated plate assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that these cells do not affect other PAG functions such as analgesia (Samineni et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic inhibition experiments in heated plate assay.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK cells selectively and bidirectionally control avoidance measures from a high-threat predator.
source: Together, these results show that, in addition to controlling avoidance measures under low-threat conditions, l/vlPAG-CCK cells also selectively and bidirectionally control avoidance measures from a high-threat predator.
evidence: Supported by both activation and inhibition experiments showing opposite effects on predator avoidance.

claim: Mean df/F of l/vlPAG-syn cells increased after open-arm entry compared to closed-arm entry in the elevated plus maze.
source: Specifically, mean df/F of l/vlPAG-syn cells increased after open-arm entry compared to closed-arm entry (Figure 8E; n = 9; t(8) = 2.856, p=0.0213).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings in the elevated plus maze.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK activity was greater following closed-arm entry compared to open-arm entry in the elevated plus maze.
source: In contrast, CCK activity was greater following closed-arm entry compared to open-arm entry (Figure 8F; n = 11; t(10) = 2.561, p=0.0283).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings in the elevated plus maze.

claim: In the low-threat EPM, l/vlPAG-CCK activity diverged from broader l/vlPAG activity.
source: Thus, in the low-threat EPM, l/vlPAG-CCK activity diverged from broader l/vlPAG activity.
evidence: Inferred from opposite patterns of activity between syn and CCK populations in response to open versus closed arm entry.

claim: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was not differentially modulated when approaching the rat during live rat exposure.
source: Mean df/F within spatial bins of varying distances from the safe wall shows that syn-GCaMP6f activity was not differentially modulated when approaching the rat but significantly altered during escapes, with dF/F peaked when mice were most proximal to the predator and sharply reduced as mice gained distance from the predator (Figure 8H; approach: r(8) = –0.255, p=0.476; escape: r(8) = 0.932, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings during live rat exposure showing no significant correlation during approaches.

claim: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was significantly altered during escapes from the rat, with dF/F peaked when mice were most proximal to the predator and sharply reduced as mice gained distance from the predator.
source: Mean df/F within spatial bins of varying distances from the safe wall shows that syn-GCaMP6f activity was not differentially modulated when approaching the rat but significantly altered during escapes, with dF/F peaked when mice were most proximal to the predator and sharply reduced as mice gained distance from the predator (Figure 8H; approach: r(8) = –0.255, p=0.476; escape: r(8) = 0.932, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing strong positive correlation between activity and proximity to predator during escapes.

claim: In CCK-GCaMP6f mice, population activity was modulated during both approaches and escapes during live rat exposure.
source: Conversely, in CCK-GCaMP6f mice, population activity was modulated during both approaches and escapes. CCK+ activity ramped down as mice moved closer to the rat and ramped up as mice escaped away from the rat (Figure 8I; approach: r(8) = –0.792, p=0.006; escape: r(8) = –0.703, p=0.023).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing significant correlations during both approaches and escapes.

claim: CCK+ activity ramped down as mice moved closer to the rat and ramped up as mice escaped away from the rat.
source: Conversely, in CCK-GCaMP6f mice, population activity was modulated during both approaches and escapes. CCK+ activity ramped down as mice moved closer to the rat and ramped up as mice escaped away from the rat (Figure 8I; approach: r(8) = –0.792, p=0.006; escape: r(8) = –0.703, p=0.023).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing negative correlation with distance from safe wall.

claim: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was tightly time-locked with escapes, increasing prior to and peaking soon after escape initiation.
source: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was tightly time-locked with escapes, increasing prior to and peaking soon after escape initiation. CCK+ activity also increased prior to escape but exhibited sustained heightened activity post-escape onset (Figure 8J and K).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing temporal dynamics of activity around escape events.

claim: CCK+ activity increased prior to escape but exhibited sustained heightened activity post-escape onset.
source: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was tightly time-locked with escapes, increasing prior to and peaking soon after escape initiation. CCK+ activity also increased prior to escape but exhibited sustained heightened activity post-escape onset (Figure 8J and K).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing temporal dynamics of CCK activity around escape events.

claim: Syn-GCaMP6f activity was greater in the threat zone than safe zone during live rat exposure.
source: Finally, syn-GCaMP6f activity was greater in the threat zone than safe zone (Figure 8L; n = 9; t(8) = 4.375, p=0.0024) while CCK-GCaMP6f activity was decreased in the threat zone relative to the safe zone (Figure 8M; n = 12; t(11) = 2.658, p=0.0223).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings comparing activity in different zones.

claim: CCK-GCaMP6f activity was decreased in the threat zone relative to the safe zone during live rat exposure.
source: Finally, syn-GCaMP6f activity was greater in the threat zone than safe zone (Figure 8L; n = 9; t(8) = 4.375, p=0.0024) while CCK-GCaMP6f activity was decreased in the threat zone relative to the safe zone (Figure 8M; n = 12; t(11) = 2.658, p=0.0223).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings comparing activity in different zones.

claim: The syn-expressing l/vlPAG population was particularly attuned to more threatening aspects of both the EPM and live predator exposure.
source: Together, these results suggest that though the syn-expressing l/vlPAG population was particularly attuned to more threatening aspects of both the EPM and live predator exposure, CCK population activity was negatively modulated by threat proximity and increased during escape movements away from threat.
evidence: Inferred from photometry data showing increased syn activity in open arms and threat zones.

claim: CCK population activity was negatively modulated by threat proximity and increased during escape movements away from threat.
source: Together, these results suggest that though the syn-expressing l/vlPAG population was particularly attuned to more threatening aspects of both the EPM and live predator exposure, CCK population activity was negatively modulated by threat proximity and increased during escape movements away from threat.
evidence: Supported by photometry data showing decreased CCK activity near threat and increased activity during escapes.

claim: l/vlPAG CCK+ cells are a key driver of the threat avoidance behavioral state.
source: We thus propose that l/vlPAG CCK+ cells are a key driver of the threat avoidance behavioral state.
evidence: Inferred from activation, inhibition, and photometry data showing CCK cells are active during avoidance and necessary for avoidance behaviors.

claim: Prior work indicates that the ventrolateral (vl) PAG column is necessary for conditioned freezing.
source: Prior work indicates that the ventrolateral (vl) PAG column is necessary for conditioned freezing (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetic and electrical excitation of the lateral (l) PAG column produces freezing.
source: Though less studied than the vlPAG, optogenetic and electrical excitation of the lateral (l) PAG column also produces freezing (Assareh et al., 2016; Bittencourt et al., 2005; Bittencourt et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The dorsolateral (dl) PAG has a key role in controlling innate defensive behaviors.
source: The dorsolateral (dl) PAG has a key role in controlling innate defensive behaviors. Indeed, dlPAG cells encode numerous defense behaviors, including freezing, escape, and risk assessment (Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009; Deng et al., 2016; Reis et al., 2021a; Reis et al., 2021b), and activation of glutamatergic vGlut2+ dlPAG cells induces escape (Evans et al., 2018; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activation of glutamatergic vGlut2+ dlPAG cells induces escape.
source: The dorsolateral (dl) PAG has a key role in controlling innate defensive behaviors. Indeed, dlPAG cells encode numerous defense behaviors, including freezing, escape, and risk assessment (Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009; Deng et al., 2016; Reis et al., 2021a; Reis et al., 2021b), and activation of glutamatergic vGlut2+ dlPAG cells induces escape (Evans et al., 2018; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PAG neurons expressing CaMKIIa elicited both freezing and flight.
source: For example, optogenetic activation of PAG neurons expressing CaMKIIa, which is ubiquitous in the region, elicited both freezing and flight (Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Intra-PAG infusion of CCK in rats induces defensive behaviors and potentiates one-way escape behavior.
source: Intriguingly, intra-PAG infusion of CCK in rats induces defensive behaviors and potentiates one-way escape behavior (Netto and Guimarães, 2004; Zanoveli et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: CCK excites PAG neurons at both pre- and postsynaptic loci.
source: Additionally, CCK excites PAG neurons at both pre- and postsynaptic loci (Liu et al., 1994; Yang et al., 2006), suggesting that PAG-CCK cells may have widespread effects on local cell activity dynamics.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: PAG-CCK cells may have widespread effects on local cell activity dynamics.
source: Additionally, CCK excites PAG neurons at both pre- and postsynaptic loci (Liu et al., 1994; Yang et al., 2006), suggesting that PAG-CCK cells may have widespread effects on local cell activity dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from prior work showing CCK excites PAG neurons at multiple loci.

claim: PAG cells are activated by proximity to danger.
source: Furthermore, though decades of prior work has consistently shown that PAG cells are activated by proximity to danger (Aguiar and Guimarães, 2009; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018; Mobbs et al., 2010; Mobbs et al., 2007; Watson et al., 2016), we find that l/vlPAG-CCK cells are more active far from threat.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior published works.

claim: l/vlPAG-CCK cells are more active far from threat.
source: Furthermore, though decades of prior work has consistently shown that PAG cells are activated by proximity to danger (Aguiar and Guimarães, 2009; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018; Mobbs et al., 2010; Mobbs et al., 2007; Watson et al., 2016), we find that l/vlPAG-CCK cells are more active far from threat.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing increased CCK activity in safe zones and during escapes away from threat.

claim: CCK cells in several brain regions such as cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala are reported to be inhibitory.
source: CCK cells in several brain regions such as cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala are reported to be inhibitory (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Mascagni and McDonald, 2003; Nguyen et al., 2020; Whissell et al., 2015), though glutamatergic CCK+ cells have also been reported in other regions (Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Glutamatergic CCK+ cells have been reported in some brain regions.
source: CCK cells in several brain regions such as cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala are reported to be inhibitory (Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Mascagni and McDonald, 2003; Nguyen et al., 2020; Whissell et al., 2015), though glutamatergic CCK+ cells have also been reported in other regions (Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Following predator exposure, the rodent PAG exhibits increased Fos expression.
source: Following predator exposure, the rodent PAG exhibits increased Fos expression (Aguiar and Guimarães, 2009; Canteras and Goto, 1999; Mendes-Gomes et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of NMDA receptors in the dorsal or ventrolateral PAG increased open arm exploration in the EPM.
source: Pharmacological blockade of NMDA receptors in the dorsal or ventrolateral PAG increased open arm exploration in the EPM (Guimarães et al., 1991; Molchanov and Guimarães, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Single-unit recordings show that dPAG and vPAG units display significant increases in firing rate after exposure to cat odor.
source: Single-unit recordings show that dPAG and vPAG units display significant increases in firing rate after exposure to cat odor (Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The dPAG is sensitive to sensory aspects of threat distance and intensity, displaying increased activity with greater proximity to an awake predator.
source: Moreover, the dPAG is sensitive to sensory aspects of threat distance and intensity, displaying increased activity with greater proximity to an awake predator (Deng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: In humans, PAG activity is positively correlated with threat imminence.
source: In humans, PAG activity is positively correlated with threat imminence (Mobbs et al., 2010; Mobbs et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Within the dPAG, glutamatergic neurons are key for escape initiation and vigor.
source: Within the dPAG, glutamatergic neurons are key for escape initiation and vigor, and dPAG flight-related cells exhibited prominent firing early during flight and declined as mice fled further from a predator (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: dPAG flight-related cells exhibited prominent firing early during flight and declined as mice fled further from a predator.
source: Within the dPAG, glutamatergic neurons are key for escape initiation and vigor, and dPAG flight-related cells exhibited prominent firing early during flight and declined as mice fled further from a predator (Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Electrical or optogenetic excitation of the lPAG or vlPAG produced freezing.
source: Pan-neuronal optogenetic activation of l/vlPAG cells produced strong freezing (Figure 2J), in agreement with prior reports showing that electrical or optogenetic excitation of the lPAG or vlPAG produced freezing (Assareh et al., 2016; Bittencourt et al., 2005; Bittencourt et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons powerfully elicited freezing.
source: Furthermore, activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons powerfully elicited freezing (Tovote et al., 2016), and vlPAG lesions curtailed freezing during predator exposure and conditioned fear (de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019; Fanselow et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: vlPAG lesions curtailed freezing during predator exposure and conditioned fear.
source: Furthermore, activation of glutamatergic vlPAG neurons powerfully elicited freezing (Tovote et al., 2016), and vlPAG lesions curtailed freezing during predator exposure and conditioned fear (de Andrade Rufino et al., 2019; Fanselow et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The PAG participates in relaying aversive unconditioned stimulus information to the amygdala to inform associative plasticity.
source: Prior data have suggested that the PAG participates in relaying aversive unconditioned stimulus information to the amygdala to inform associative plasticity, and this feature is critical to prediction error coding (Herry and Johansen, 2014; Johansen et al., 2010; McNally et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: vlPAG neurons have a role in prediction error coding.
source: Though studies have identified a role of vlPAG neurons in prediction error coding (Ozawa et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2020), our inhibition of CCK+ cells during fear acquisition did not alter freezing during acquisition nor retrieval, suggesting that a role in prediction error coding may be carried out by other vlPAG cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Dorsal PAG stimulation in rodents has been shown to induce marked escape responses such as explosive vertical jumping, running, aversion, and panic-related sympathetic responses.
source: Dorsal PAG stimulation in rodents has been shown to induce marked escape responses such as explosive vertical jumping, running, aversion, and panic-related sympathetic responses (Del-Ben and Graeff, 2009; Depaulis et al., 1992; Fanselow, 1991; Jenck et al., 1995; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Valenstein, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Broad activation of the dorsolateral column induces flight, hypertension, and tachycardia, while activation of the ventrolateral column induces freezing, hypotension, and bradycardia.
source: Broad activation of the dorsolateral column induces flight, hypertension, and tachycardia, while activation of the ventrolateral column induces freezing, hypotension, and bradycardia (Keay and Bandler, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work summarizing columnar organization.

claim: Adrenergic and noradrenergic medullary afferents preferentially target the rostral vlPAG.
source: For example, adrenergic and noradrenergic medullary afferents preferentially target the rostral vlPAG and the central amygdala receives input from cells highly concentrated in the caudal but not rostral vlPAG (Silva and McNaughton, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The central amygdala receives input from cells highly concentrated in the caudal but not rostral vlPAG.
source: For example, adrenergic and noradrenergic medullary afferents preferentially target the rostral vlPAG and the central amygdala receives input from cells highly concentrated in the caudal but not rostral vlPAG (Silva and McNaughton, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: GABA-immunopositive cells are more prevalent in caudal than rostral cat vlPAG.
source: Furthermore, there are genetic markers that do not span an entire column; GABA-immunopositive cells are more prevalent in caudal than rostral cat vlPAG (Barbaresi, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Inhibition of lPAG VGAT and lPAG VGlut2+ neurons impairs the chase and attack of prey, respectively.
source: Indeed, inhibition of lPAG VGAT and lPAG VGlut2+ neurons impairs the chase and attack of prey, respectively (Yu et al., 2021), and glutamatergic vlPAG neurons project to the medulla to control freezing (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Glutamatergic vlPAG neurons project to the medulla to control freezing.
source: Indeed, inhibition of lPAG VGAT and lPAG VGlut2+ neurons impairs the chase and attack of prey, respectively (Yu et al., 2021), and glutamatergic vlPAG neurons project to the medulla to control freezing (Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: l/vlPAG tac1+ cells specifically control itching behavior.
source: Moreover, l/vlPAG tac1+ cells have been shown to specifically control itching behavior (Gao et al., 2019), further supporting the value of investigating sparse genetically defined PAG populations.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: l/vlPAG CCK+ cells have opposing function and neural activation motifs compared to the broader local ensemble defined solely by columnar boundaries.
source: Thus, CCK l/vlPAG cells have opposing function and neural activation motifs compared to the broader local ensemble defined solely by columnar boundaries.
evidence: Supported by data showing CCK cells drive flight while pan-neuronal l/vlPAG drives freezing, and CCK cells are more active far from threat while pan-neuronal cells are more active near threat.

claim: The molecular identity of PAG cells may confer an additional axis of functional organization.
source: In addition to the anatomical columnar architecture of the PAG, the molecular identity of PAG cells may confer an additional axis of functional organization, revealing unexplored functional heterogeneity.
evidence: Inferred from findings showing CCK cells have distinct functions from pan-neuronal populations in the same anatomical region.

claim: CCK cells drive threat avoidance states, which are epochs during which mice increase distance from threat and perform evasive escape.
source: These results suggest CCK cells drive threat avoidance states, which are epochs during which mice increase distance from threat and perform evasive escape.
evidence: Inferred from activation, inhibition, and photometry data showing CCK cells control avoidance behaviors and are active during avoidance.

claim: l/vlPAG CCK+ cells control avoidance of threat in multiple contexts.
source: Our study identifies a small, sparse, genetically defined subset of cells within the PAG, cholecystokinin-expressing neurons (CCK+) that control avoidance of threat in multiple contexts.
evidence: Supported by data from multiple behavioral assays showing CCK cells control avoidance in both low-threat and high-threat environments.

claim: Activation of l/vlPAG CCK+ cells induced evasion of open spaces and a live predator.
source: Activation of l/vlPAG CCK+ cells induced evasion of open spaces and a live predator, which are, respectively, low- and high-intensity threats.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments in open field and live predator exposure assays.

claim: Inhibition of CCK+ cells delayed entry into a dark burrow and increased time spent near a live predator.
source: Conversely, inhibition of CCK+ cells delayed entry into a dark burrow and increased time spent near a live predator, showing that these cells bidirectionally control avoidance measures in both low- and high-threat environments.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic and chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: CCK+ cells display increased activity with greater threat avoidance in both the low-threat EPM and the high-threat predator exposure.
source: CCK+ cells also display increased activity with greater threat avoidance in both the low-threat EPM and the high-threat predator exposure.
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry recordings showing increased CCK activity in closed arms of EPM and in safe zones during predator exposure.

claim: Pan-neuronal activation of the same lPAG and vlPAG region drove robust freezing.
source: We show that these features are specific to CCK+ cells and oppose the broader local ensemble, as pan-neuronal activation of the same lPAG and vlPAG region drove robust freezing (Figure 2J), and pan-neuronal activation patterns show increased activity with greater threat proximity (Figure 8L), consistent with prior reports (Assareh et al., 2016; Bittencourt et al., 2005; Deng et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2018; Mobbs et al., 2010; Mobbs et al., 2007; Reis et al., 2021a; Tovote et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation experiments and citations to prior work.

claim: l/vlPAG CCK+ cells are selectively driving and signaling a behavioral state of threat avoidance and diverges from pan-neuronal l/vlPAG function.
source: Together, these data suggest that l/vlPAG CCK+ cells are selectively driving and signaling a behavioral state of threat avoidance and diverges from pan-neuronal l/vlPAG function.
evidence: Inferred from data showing CCK cells have distinct behavioral effects and activity patterns compared to pan-neuronal l/vlPAG populations.

claim: This is the first PAG cell type identified in which endogenous activity is reduced with threat proximity.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first PAG cell type identified in which endogenous activity is reduced with threat proximity.
evidence: Based on comparison with prior literature showing PAG cells are typically more active near threat, and current data showing CCK cells are less active near threat.

claim: The identification of l/vlPAG CCK+ neurons as a population that drives escape, rather than freezing, opposes the canonical function of this region.
source: The identification of l/vlPAG CCK+ neurons as a population that drives escape, rather than freezing, thus opposes the canonical function of this region.
evidence: Inferred from data showing CCK cells drive escape while prior work and current pan-neuronal data show l/vlPAG drives freezing.

claim: The flight pattern observed from l/vlPAG CCK+ activation is characteristically different from escape canonically described in PAG studies as they are void of robust protean vertical jumping seen in dlPAG activation.
source: Interestingly, the flight pattern observed from l/vlPAG CCK+ activation is characteristically different from escape canonically described in PAG studies as they are void of robust protean vertical jumping seen in dlPAG activation in this study (Figure 2I) and prior work (Ullah et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by comparison of behavioral phenotypes between CCK activation and dlPAG activation.

claim: There are two distinct types of escape: flight to escape the environment as seen by jumps induced by pan-neuronal activation of dlPAG cells and flight to safer regions within the environment, as shown by l/vlPAG CCK+ cell activation.
source: Therefore, our work draws attention to two distinct types of escape: flight to escape the environment as seen by jumps induced by pan-neuronal activation of dlPAG cells (Figure 2I) and flight to safer regions within the environment, as shown by l/vlPAG CCK+ cell activation (Figures 2–3 and 6).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of behavioral phenotypes between dlPAG and CCK activation.

claim: Deciphering how molecularly defined PAG populations complement and interact with the well-established anatomical columnar functional framework is a key step in understanding how this ancient structure controls a constellation of vital behaviors.
source: Deciphering how molecularly defined PAG populations complement and interact with the well-established anatomical columnar functional framework is a key step in understanding how this ancient structure controls a constellation of vital behaviors.
evidence: This is a perspective statement based on the findings of the study.
